title: A New Heart, and the Glory Departs
summary: At the east gate of the temple Ezekiel sees twenty-five leaders who boast that Jerusalem is a cooking pot and they are the choice meat, safe inside it. He prophesies against them, and one of them, Pelatiah, dies. God then promises the exiles, whom Jerusalem had written off, that he has been a sanctuary for them, that he will gather them, and that he will give them a new heart and spirit. The glory of the LORD leaves the city and stands on the mountain to the east, and Ezekiel is carried back to Babylon.
story: Chapter 11 ends the temple vision that began in chapter 8, and it turns the book's direction. Up to now Ezekiel's message has been almost entirely judgment. Here, for the first time, comes a full promise of restoration, and it is given not to the people in Jerusalem, who thought they were God's favored ones, but to the exiles in Babylon, whom Jerusalem despised. The glory of God, which had moved step by step from the inner sanctuary (9:3) to the east gate (10:19), now leaves the city entirely (verse 23). The temple is empty of God's presence. The book will not see that glory return until chapter 43, when it comes back through the same east gate into a renewed temple.
historical:
After the deportation of 597 BC, those left in Jerusalem apparently told themselves that they were the true Israel and that the exiles, far away from the LORD, had lost their share in the land (verse 15). Property left behind by deported families may have passed into the hands of those who stayed. Jeremiah answered the same attitude with his vision of two baskets of figs, in which the good figs were the exiles and the bad were King Zedekiah and his officials in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 24).

The two leaders named here, Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, are otherwise unknown. This Jaazaniah is a different man from Jaazaniah son of Shaphan in 8:11. Pelatiah's death during the vision (verse 13) is reported as something Ezekiel saw happen as he prophesied; the text does not explain whether it also took place at that moment in Jerusalem, and interpreters differ on that question. The glory's final stop, “the mountain east of the city” (verse 23), is the Mount of Olives, which overlooks Jerusalem from across the Kidron Valley.
cultural:
The leaders' proverb, “The city is the cooking pot, and we are the meat” (verse 3), used a household image. A cooking pot protects the meat inside from the fire beneath it, and the choice portions were the best part of an animal. The leaders meant that Jerusalem's walls would protect them and that they were the prime cut of the nation, while the exiles were the scraps thrown away. Their other saying, that it was time to build houses, likely expressed confidence that life would continue as normal; Jeremiah had told the exiles to build houses in Babylon (Jeremiah 29:5), not those in Jerusalem. God turns their image around: the only real meat in the pot is the people they have killed (verse 7).

The word translated “your relatives” in verse 15 comes from the Hebrew for redemption. In Israelite family law a close relative was responsible for redeeming land or persons that had been lost (Leviticus 25:25). The phrase suggests that the exiles were the very people whose property the Jerusalemites should have protected, and instead had taken.
literary: The chapter has two oracles, one of judgment (verses 1 to 13) and one of promise (verses 14 to 21), followed by the conclusion of the whole vision (verses 22 to 25). The first oracle quotes the leaders' words and then turns them against them. The second quotes what Jerusalem says about the exiles and then answers it. Each oracle ends at a point of crisis: the first with Pelatiah's death and Ezekiel's cry for the remnant (verse 13), echoing his cry in 9:8; the second with the promise of a new heart, which answers that cry. The promise in verses 19 and 20 is repeated almost exactly in 36:26-28 and ends with the covenant formula, “they will be My people, and I will be their God,” which runs through the whole Bible.

outline.t: Twenty-five leaders and their proverb of the pot
The city is not your shelter: judgment on the leaders
Pelatiah dies, and the prophet cries out
God has been a sanctuary for the exiles
Gathering, cleansing, and a new heart
The glory leaves the city, and the prophet returns to the exiles

doctrines.note: The new heart and new spirit are God's gift, not Israel's achievement. God removes the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh so that his people can obey. Restoration begins with an inward change that only God can bring about.

The closing formula, “they will be My people, and I will be their God” (verse 20), is the heart of God's covenant from Exodus onward. Judgment has not cancelled the covenant; God will renew it with a remade people.

Ezekiel is moved and instructed by the Spirit throughout the chapter (verses 1, 5, 24), and God promises to put “a new spirit” within his people (verse 19). The same Spirit who inspires the prophet will renew the people, a promise Ezekiel develops in 36:27 and 37:14.

words.note: Lev, heart. In Hebrew thought the heart is not mainly the seat of feelings but the center of thought, will, and decision. A heart of stone is one that cannot respond to God; a heart of flesh is alive and responsive. The promise is a new inner self, not merely new behavior.

Ruach, spirit, wind, or breath. The same word describes the Spirit who lifts Ezekiel (verse 1) and the new spirit God will put in his people (verse 19). Ezekiel moves easily between God's Spirit and the renewed human spirit, because the second comes from the first.

Miqdash, sanctuary. In verse 16 God says that he has been a sanctuary for the exiles “for a little while.” The Hebrew can also be read as a sanctuary in small measure. Either way, God himself is present to his scattered people, even without a temple.

Ge'ullah, redemption, the right or duty of a close relative to buy back family land or free a family member. The BSB renders the phrase in verse 15 as “your relatives.” The word hints that the exiles are family members owed care, not strangers to be dispossessed.

christ: The promise of a new heart and spirit stands alongside Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-34), and the New Testament sees both fulfilled through Christ and the gift of the Spirit. Jesus told Nicodemus that a person must be born of water and the Spirit (John 3:5), language that many interpreters connect with Ezekiel's promises, and Paul describes believers as a letter written with the Spirit of the living God on tablets of human hearts (2 Corinthians 3:3). The glory's departure to the Mount of Olives is also suggestive: Zechariah 14:4 pictures the LORD standing on that mountain in the last day, and Luke records that Jesus ascended from the vicinity of Bethany and the Mount of Olives (Luke 24:50-51; Acts 1:12). That last connection is thematic, and the New Testament does not draw it explicitly.

hard.q: Did Pelatiah really die because of Ezekiel's prophecy, and why would God strike him down?
hard.a: The text reports that Pelatiah died while Ezekiel was prophesying in his vision. Some interpreters take it as an event Ezekiel later learned had actually happened in Jerusalem, a confirmation that his visions were real. Others think Pelatiah's death belongs within the vision, a visionary sign of what was coming for the leaders. The text does not settle the question. What it does make clear is Ezekiel's reaction: not satisfaction but alarm, as he cries out, “will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end?” The death shows that the word of God is not idle talk, and the prophet's cry leads directly to God's answer: a remnant will be gathered and given a new heart.

questions: The leaders in Jerusalem saw themselves as the prime cut and the exiles as scraps. Where are you tempted to measure God's favor by your security or success?
God told the exiles he had been a sanctuary for them without a temple. What does it mean for you that God can be present in places of loss and displacement?
What would it look like for God to replace a heart of stone with a heart of flesh in an area of your life that has become hard?
